title: Sticky-Rice Soup Holds Up Nanjing's 600-Year-Old Ming Wall | China Travel Expert
description:
Sticky-rice soup is one reason Nanjing's 600-year-old city wall is still standing.

Analysis of the mortar in Nanjing's roughly 600-year-old Ming city wall found it was made of slaked lime mixed with glutinous ('sticky') rice soup. The tell-tale sign was amylopectin, the starch in the rice. In a 2010 study (Accounts of Chemical Research), a team led by Zhang Bingjian showed the starch controls how the lime's calcium carbonate crystallises, producing a denser, more water-resistant and crack-resistant mortar. The technique is about 1,500 years old and was used in Ming walls, tombs and pagodas. One researcher told National Geographic the mortar's strength is only 'average' — so whether it's genius or overrated is a real debate.

🧭 Expert Tip: start at Zhonghua Gate (Zhonghuamen), the wall's grandest fortress gate, then walk the ramparts toward the old city.

南京约600年的明城墙砂浆里，检出了糯米汤的支链淀粉——糯米灰浆让石灰的碳酸钙结晶更致密、更抗水，这项技术约有1500年历史。不过有研究者说它的强度只是“一般”。
